author: Ben Morris
title: How the government shutdown is already affecting Central Valley workers, recreation - NewsBreak
text:
By Ben Morris ,
1 hours ago FRESNO COUNTY, Calif. ( KSEE/KGPE ) – A stalemate between Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill has already started to impact those working and living in California’s Central Valley.
Many who have already started to feel the pain firsthand are essential federal workers, such as those within the Federal Bureau of Prisons.
“Our staff do a very dangerous job. They put their lives on the line every single day working with these offenders and they don’t know when they’re going to get paid and when they’re going to be able to take care of their family and put food on their table,” said Aaron McGlothlin, the president of AFGE CPL-33 Local 1237, the union representing prison workers at the Federal Correctional Institution in Mendota.
McGlothin says from Wednesday until the shutdown ends, prison workers there, and other essential government employees around the region, state, and country, will have to continue working without pay.
While he says they would eventually get back pay, they, in particular, have been hit with a double whammy after the Federal Bureau of Prisons canceled union Collective Bargaining Agreements less than a week before the shutdown started on Sept. 25.
He says that stripped workers of vital workplace rights and protections, such as shift bidding, seniority, and safeguards to working conditions, overtime, safety, and due process.
While McGlothin says they have a court hearing on Oct. 20 seeking an injunction, workers still have to show up each day, now without pay.
He’s calling on both Republicans and Democrats to reach an agreement so workers don’t have to continue living with fear of the unknown.
“It’s on both sides of the aisle. They need to come together and find common ground because they forget about the people that are still doing the hard work on the ground and put their life on the line every single day,” he said.
Dr. Thomas Holyoke, a political science professor at Fresno State, says if an agreement isn’t reached soon, both parties will begin to feel political pain.
“After some time goes by, both parties are going to see their poll numbers deteriorate on this. The public does not like it when the government gets shut down because that means, increasingly, services the public kind of assumes they’re going to get, aren’t coming.”
Meanwhile, at the National Park Service, roughly two-thirds of employees were furloughed at the start of the shutdown, although many parks, like Yosemite, will remain open.
“Our parks are open, the gates are open, but there’s just not adequate staff and resources available to keep an eye on the thousands and thousands of acres and the resources within our parks,” said Sierra Nevada Sr. Program Manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, Mark Rose.
Rose’s nationwide organization, the NPCA, is growing more and more worried about the shutdown because of what happened during the last shutdown from Dec. 2018 to Jan. 2019.
At that time, he says, parks were left in a shocking state with employees and many essential services no longer on the grounds.
“During that period, the parks were heavily impacted by stuff like human waste and trash building up. There were certain areas that they ended up having to close because of public safety concerns,” Rose said.
According to the Yosemite Mariposa County Tourism Bureau, entry fees will not be collected at Yosemite during the shutdown. We are continuing to find out whether the impacts will look the same at Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks.
